# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Gap Analysis and Roadmap

## Corrections to my earlier notes
- **ITIL access management:** I listed "Access management" as an ITIL 4 practice. ITIL 4 has no standalone practice by that name (it was an ITIL v3 process). Access is handled through **Information security management** and **Service request management**. The mapping below uses those.
- **Stage 1 audit:** I called it a "readiness assessment." Stage 1 is a formal part of certification, a documentation and readiness review that can raise findings. If you want a non-binding dry run, ask the certification body (CB) for a separate pre-assessment, or use a consultant.

## Assumptions
- Ratings below are inferred from your summary, not from an audit. Treat them as hypotheses to validate.
- **Regulator is unknown.** For a regional financial firm (GLBA/FFIEC/NYDFS, PCI DSS, or non-US equivalents), your legal and regulatory register (5.31) must reflect it, and some regulatory controls may outrank ISO priorities.
- Physical security, HR processes, and secure development weren't described, so I've marked them "unknown."
- Scope: the whole organization's IT services (Azure, VMware, SaaS, legacy apps). Narrowing scope can save time but is hard to justify for a 250-person firm.
- Priorities: **P1** = blocks certification or is high risk, **P2** = needed before Stage 2, **P3** = refine and sustain.

---

## 1. Gap-analysis checklist

### A. ISMS management clauses (4–10)
These are mandatory, and missing them is the most common cause of major nonconformities.

| Clause | Requirement | Likely status | Priority | ITIL leverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1–4.4 | Context, interested parties, scope, ISMS | Gap | P1 | Service portfolio |
| 5.1–5.3 | Leadership commitment, security policy, roles | Partial (some policies) | P1 | Governance, if documented |
| 6.1.2 | Documented risk assessment method and criteria | **Gap** | P1 | Risk management practice |
| 6.1.3 | Risk treatment plan and **Statement of Applicability** | **Gap** | P1 | None |
| 6.2 | Measurable security objectives | Gap | P2 | Continual improvement |
| 7.2–7.4 | Competence, awareness, communication | Partial | P2 | Workforce and talent management |
| 7.5 | Documented information control | Partial | P2 | Knowledge management |
| 8.1–8.3 | Operate risk assessment and treatment on schedule | Gap | P1 | None |
| 9.1 | Metrics, monitoring, measurement | Gap | P2 | Service level management |
| 9.2 | **Internal audit** of the ISMS | Gap | P1 | None |
| 9.3 | **Management review** | Gap | P1 | None |
| 10.1–10.2 | Nonconformity and corrective action | Partial | P2 | Problem management, continual improvement |

### B. Annex A controls (93 controls, four themes)

**Organizational (5.x)**

| Controls | Area | Likely status | Priority | ITIL practice / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1, 5.37 | Policies, documented procedures | Partial | P2 | Needs a full policy set (access, crypto, backup, supplier, etc.) |
| 5.2, 5.3 | Roles, segregation of duties | Unknown | P2 | Check admin vs. approver separation in change |
| 5.9 | Asset inventory | **Incomplete CMDB** | P1 | Service configuration management |
| 5.10, 5.11 | Acceptable use, return of assets | Partial | P2 | AUP exists |
| 5.12, 5.13 | Data classification and labelling | Likely gap | P1 | Critical for PII and financial data |
| 5.15, 5.16, 5.18 | Access control, identity, access rights review | **Gap** | P1 | Information security management, service request management |
| 5.19–5.22 | Supplier security, agreements, monitoring | **Gap** (inconsistent clauses) | P1 | Supplier management |
| 5.23 | Cloud services security | Gap | P1 | Azure and SaaS shared-responsibility records |
| 5.24–5.28 | Incident management | Partial (ITIL incident) | P2 | Incident management. Add security-incident classification, evidence handling, and lessons learned |
| 5.29, 5.30 | Security in disruption, ICT continuity | Gap | P1 | Service continuity management. Needs BIA, RTO/RPO, and tests |
| 5.31, 5.34 | Legal/regulatory register, PII protection | Likely gap | P1 | Compliance register |
| 5.35, 5.36 | Independent review, policy compliance | Gap | P2 | Ties to the internal audit |

**People (6.x)**

| Controls | Area | Status | Priority | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1, 6.2, 6.5, 6.6 | Screening, terms, offboarding, NDAs | Unknown (HR-owned) | P2 | Offboarding must trigger access removal |
| 6.3 | Awareness and training | Gap | P1 | Role-based, with records |
| 6.7 | Remote working | Partial | P2 | Needs BYOD policy finalized |
| 6.8 | Security event reporting | Partial | P2 | Reuse the service desk channel |

**Physical (7.x)**

| Controls | Area | Status | Priority | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1–7.4 | Perimeter, entry, offices, monitoring | Unknown | P2 | Applies to on-prem VMware and office |
| 7.5, 7.8, 7.13, 7.14 | Environmental threats, equipment, maintenance, disposal | Unknown | P2 | Asset disposal records are commonly missed |

**Technological (8.x)**

| Controls | Area | Status | Priority | ITIL practice / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.1, 6.7 | Endpoint and BYOD | Partial | P1 | MDM/compliance enforcement |
| 8.2, 8.5 | Privileged access, secure authentication | **Gap** (local privileged accounts, MFA not universal) | **P1** | Move to Entra ID PIM/PAM and enforce MFA everywhere |
| 8.3 | Information access restriction | Unknown | P2 | Least privilege on data stores |
| 8.7 | Malware protection | Unknown | P2 | EDR coverage evidence |
| 8.8 | Technical vulnerability management | **Gap** (ad-hoc scans) | **P1** | Deployment and release management. Needs scheduled scanning, SLAs, and exceptions |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | Gap | P2 | Baselines and hardening standards (new in 2022) |
| 8.10, 8.11, 8.12 | Data deletion, masking, DLP | Likely gap | P2 | New in 2022. Risk-based applicability |
| 8.13 | Backup | **Partial** (restore tests infrequent) | P1 | Scheduled, documented restore tests |
| 8.14 | Redundancy | Unknown | P3 | Tied to the BIA |
| 8.15, 8.16 | Logging, monitoring | Unknown, likely partial | P1 | Monitoring and event management. Centralize logs (e.g., Sentinel) with retention and review |
| 8.20–8.22 | Network security, segregation, web filtering | Unknown | P2 | Include VMware and Azure network segmentation |
| 8.24 | Cryptography | Likely gap | P2 | Key management and encryption standard |
| 8.25–8.29, 8.31 | Secure development, environment separation | Unknown | P2 | Needed for in-house apps |
| 8.32 | Change management | Partial (ITIL change) | P2 | Change enablement. Add security-impact assessment and emergency change review |
| 8.34 | Protection during audit testing | Gap | P3 | Minor |

**Legacy on-prem apps:** these are likely your highest technical risk. Where you can't patch or upgrade them, document **risk acceptance or compensating controls** (segmentation, monitoring, restricted access) in the treatment plan. Auditors accept this, but they don't accept unmanaged risk.

---

## 2. Top priorities

1. Formal risk assessment, treatment plan, and SoA (blocks everything else)
2. Privileged access cleanup and universal MFA (highest risk and quick win)
3. Complete the asset inventory/CMDB (risk assessment depends on it)
4. Vulnerability management program with SLAs
5. Supplier risk process and contract security addendum
6. Backup restore testing and continuity (BIA, RTO/RPO)
7. Data classification, logging, and awareness training
8. Internal audit and management review, which have a hard timeline dependency

---

## 3. Roadmap (start May 2026, target certification Jan–Feb 2027)

Realistic timeline: **~8–9 months**. Six months is possible only with consultant support and early CB booking.

| Phase | Timing | Milestones | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Mobilize** | May–early Jun 2026 | Executive sponsor named, scope statement, steering committee, CB shortlisted and Stage 1/2 dates booked, regulatory register started | Signed scope and ISMS policy; CB engaged |
| **1. Foundation** | Jun–Jul | Risk methodology approved, CMDB and asset inventory completed for in-scope assets, data classification scheme, first risk assessment, **quick wins**: eliminate local privileged accounts, enforce MFA, fix BYOD policy | Risk register v1; privileged accounts in Entra ID with MFA |
| **2. Build** | Aug–Oct | Risk treatment plan and **SoA**, policy set, vulnerability management program live, supplier tiering and contract addenda, BIA and restore test, logging centralization, security incident procedure, awareness training rollout | SoA approved; policies published; first scan and restore-test evidence |
| **3. Operate and verify** | Oct–Nov | ISMS operating (records accumulating), first access review, internal audit, management review, corrective actions | Internal audit report; management review minutes; open findings tracked |
| **4. Certify** | Late Nov–Feb 2027 | Stage 1 audit, fix findings, then Stage 2 | Certificate issued after any major nonconformities are closed |

Auditors want to see the ISMS **actually operating** before Stage 2, so aim for at least ~3 months of records, including the internal audit and management review, before it.

---

## 4. Resource estimates (rough; adjust after scoping)

| Role | Estimated effort | Main tasks |
|---|---|---|
| ISMS lead (one of your 2 security/compliance staff) | ~50–60% for 9 months | Program management, risk register, SoA, audit liaison |
| Second security/compliance FTE | ~40–50% | Policies, evidence, training, supplier reviews |
| Infra/cloud and sysadmins | ~15–20% each (peak Jun–Oct) | PAM/MFA, vulnerability program, backups, logging, hardening |
| App team | ~10% | Legacy app risks, secure SDLC, change controls |
| Service desk | ~5–10% | Incident, access request, and offboarding evidence |
| HR, legal, procurement | ~5% | Onboarding/offboarding, contracts, supplier reviews |
| Executive sponsor and management | A few hours monthly plus review meetings | Approvals, resourcing, management review |

**Likely external costs** (obtain quotes, as they vary widely):
- CB audit: initial audit often runs around 10–16 audit days for an org your size, plus annual surveillance audits.
- Optional consultant for gap analysis, ISMS documentation, and internal audit support. An independent internal auditor helps, since your own team shouldn't audit controls it built.
- Tooling: vulnerability scanner, SIEM/log retention, MDM, and a GRC or policy tool if you lack one.

Your team is stretched. A 12-person IT department running daily operations alongside this is the main schedule risk.

---

## 5. Evidence auditors will expect

| Area | Typical evidence |
|---|---|
| Scope and context | Scope statement, interested-parties register, context analysis |
| Leadership | Signed ISMS policy, role assignments, objectives, management review minutes |
| Risk | Methodology, risk register with owners, treatment plan, approved SoA, risk acceptances |
| Assets and classification | Reconciled CMDB, owner assignments, classification records |
| Access | Joiner/mover/leaver tickets, access review sign-offs, privileged account list, MFA coverage report, Conditional Access policy exports |
| Vulnerability and patching | Scan schedules and reports, remediation tickets against SLAs, exception approvals |
| Change | Change records showing approval, testing, and rollback, plus emergency change reviews |
| Backup and continuity | BIA, RTO/RPO, restore test results, continuity test report |
| Logging and monitoring | Log source inventory, retention settings, alert and review records |
| Incident | Incident register with security classification, post-incident reviews, evidence of regulatory notifications if applicable |
| Suppliers | Supplier register, tiering, due diligence (SOC 2 / ISO certificates), contracts with security clauses, periodic review |
| People | Screening and onboarding checklists, training records, signed policies |
| Physical | Access logs, visitor records, equipment disposal certificates |
| Assurance | Internal audit plan, report, nonconformity log, corrective action records |

Auditors will sample records and interview staff, so people need to be able to describe what they actually do.

---

## 6. Decisions and questions

1. Which regulator(s) and frameworks apply? Their requirements may change priorities and the evidence overlap.
2. Do you have an executive sponsor with budget authority?
3. Can you accept consultant support, or must this be fully in-house?
4. What is the state of the physical environment (on-prem datacenter, office access)?
5. Is there any in-house software development?
6. Are there existing certifications or audits (SOC 2, PCI DSS) whose evidence can be reused?

If you give me answers to these, I can build the **risk register template**, a **draft SoA** with applicability rationale for each control, or a **90-day sprint plan** for Phases 0–1.

# 90-Day Sprint Plan (Phases 0-1) and Risk Register Template

## 1. Scope statement: suggested edits

Your draft is a good start. Five changes will help it survive a Stage 1 review:

1. **Personal devices:** You have a BYOD draft policy, so "excluded: non-business personal devices" is ambiguous. Exclude only personal devices that never touch firm data. BYOD devices that access email, SaaS, or files are in scope for the controls you apply (MDM, Conditional Access).
2. **Suppliers:** Clause 4.3 wants clear boundaries. Your ISMS covers how you select, contract, monitor, and exit suppliers (5.19-5.23), not their internal systems. Say that explicitly rather than "outside our contractual control," which is vague and invites questions.
3. **"Supporting financial operations":** This could be read as excluding HR or general corporate IT. Since HR SaaS holds PII, say "all information and systems the firm operates or relies on."
4. **Locations and people:** Name the HQ site and datacenter, and add remote workers and contractors.
5. **Interfaces and dependencies:** Clause 4.3 requires you to consider them, such as internet providers, Azure/Microsoft, and the regulator reporting channel.

**Proposed wording:**

> The Information Security Management System (ISMS) of [Company] covers the protection of all information assets, systems, and services that the firm operates or relies on to deliver its financial services, including the creation, processing, storage, and transmission of PII and financial data.
>
> **In scope:** the HQ office and on-premises datacenter (locked cages, badge access, CCTV); Azure tenants and subscriptions [list]; on-premises VMware infrastructure; SaaS applications (CRM [name], HR [name]); corporate-managed endpoints and personal (BYOD) devices that access firm data; cloud backups; IT operations; in-house software development; and remote working by employees and contractors.
>
> **Suppliers:** The ISMS covers supplier selection, contracting, monitoring, and exit for suppliers that process or store firm PII or financial data. Suppliers' internal systems are outside the ISMS and are addressed through supplier risk management.
>
> **Out of scope:** personal devices that do not access firm data; [any other named exclusions, each with a justification].
>
> **Interfaces and dependencies:** [e.g., internet/telecom providers, Microsoft cloud services, regulator reporting channels].

Two notes. Scope exclusions are different from "not applicable" controls in the SoA, so don't use scope to dodge controls. Also name the actual tenants, subscriptions, and applications rather than categories, because auditors will test the boundary.

# 90-Day Sprint Plan (continued) and Risk Register Template

## Correction to the earlier S2 task
I wrote that break-glass accounts should be "excluded from Conditional Access." That is outdated. Microsoft now enforces mandatory MFA for Azure admin portals and, in later phases, for CLI, PowerShell, and ARM, and break-glass accounts are not exempt. The current guidance is to use **phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 passkeys or certificate-based auth)** on 2 cloud-only break-glass accounts, monitor and alert on every sign-in, and test them periodically. Verify against Microsoft's current documentation when you configure them. Also confirm licensing early: **Entra PIM needs Entra ID P2** (or ID Governance), and Conditional Access needs P1 or higher.

---

## 2. Risk methodology (copy into your policy doc)

**Information Security Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology**
Version 0.1 | Owner: ISMS Lead | Approver: Steering Committee | Review: annually

**2.1 Purpose and scope**
This methodology defines how [Company] identifies, analyzes, evaluates, treats, and accepts information security risks across the ISMS scope, in line with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clauses 6.1.2, 6.1.3, and 8.2-8.3. It applies to all risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information assets.

**2.2 Roles**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Executive Sponsor | Accepts High risks. Sets risk appetite with the steering committee. |
| CEO | Accepts Critical risks (funded plan required). |
| Steering Committee | Approves this methodology. Reviews High and Critical risks. |
| ISMS Lead | Maintains the register and process. Verifies the methodology was followed. |
| Risk Owner | Accountable for the risk and its treatment. Accepts Low and Medium risks. |
| Asset Owner | Confirms business impact and service constraints. |

**2.3 Process**
Identify (by asset or service, using threat and vulnerability) → analyze (inherent likelihood × impact) → evaluate against the bands → choose treatment (mitigate, accept, transfer, avoid) → score residual risk after treatment → obtain approval at the required authority level → monitor and review.

**2.4 Likelihood scale**

| Score | Level | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | Less than once in 5+ years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Once in 3-5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Once in 1-3 years |
| 4 | Likely | About once a year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Multiple times a year |

**2.5 Impact scale (score by the highest applicable dimension)**

| Score | Data / regulatory | Financial [set with Finance] | Operational | Reputation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Negligible | No exposure | < [$X] | No service impact | None |
| 2 Minor | Internal data only, no notification | [$X-$Y] | < 4 hours, non-critical service | Internal awareness only |
| 3 Moderate | Limited non-sensitive exposure | [$Y-$Z] | Up to 1 business day, or a critical service degraded | Limited customer complaints |
| 4 Major | PII/financial exposure, regulator notification required | [$Z-$W] | Multi-day outage of a critical service | Local media or notable customer loss |
| 5 Severe | Large-scale breach, regulatory action or sanction | > [$W] | Extended outage, inability to operate | Loss of trust, significant customer attrition |

**2.6 Scoring and bands**
Score = Likelihood × Impact.

| Band | Score | Treatment expectation | Acceptance authority | Max acceptance period | Review |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 1-4 | Accept or monitor | Risk Owner | 12 months | Annually |
| Medium | 5-9 | Treat where cost-effective | Risk Owner, ISMS Lead informed | 12 months | Every 6 months |
| High | 10-16 | Treatment plan required | Executive Sponsor | 12 months | Quarterly |
| Critical | 20-25 | Immediate action and funded plan | CEO | 6 months | Monthly |

A High or Critical impact score of 4 or 5 on the data/regulatory dimension must also be referred to Legal/Compliance to check notification obligations.

**2.7 Risk appetite statements**
1. [Company] has **very low appetite** for unauthorized disclosure, loss, or alteration of Restricted data (PII and financial data).
2. [Company] has **no appetite** for unmanaged risk. Every risk above Medium must have an owner and a documented decision.
3. **Critical risks are not accepted** unless a funded remediation plan exists, and then only for up to 6 months.
4. [Company] has **low appetite** for prolonged outages of critical financial services beyond the RTOs set in the BIA.
5. Legacy or unsupported systems handling Restricted data are tolerated only with documented compensating controls, a replacement plan, and time-limited acceptance.
6. [Company] will meet all legal and regulatory notification obligations. This is not subject to risk acceptance.

**2.8 Review triggers**
Review the full register at least annually. Also review after any significant incident, major change (new system, supplier, or acquisition), change in law or regulation, or a failed control test. Overdue treatment actions must be re-dated with a recorded reason.
